Test everything on one bench

Plug a device in and its card lights up. Controllers and wheels are scored the second they connect. Nothing is uploaded — every test runs inside this tab. Press Ctrl+K anywhere to jump straight to a test without reaching for the mouse — it works even while capture mode is holding the keyboard.

Detected now

Live controller scoreboard

This browser

A controller stays invisible to every browser until it sends one input — that is a browser rule, not a fault with the pad. If a card stays dark, press a face button.

Unit report

Everything you test in this tab is recorded as you go. Fill in the unit details and this turns the session into a one-page QC record you can print, save as a PDF, or paste straight into a listing or a returns dispute. It is built from the results themselves, not typed up afterwards — so it says what the bench actually found, including the parts that failed.

nothing recorded yet

CSV gives one row per test with the unit, grade and operator repeated on every line, so it drops straight into an inventory sheet and filters properly. The untested pages get rows too, with an empty score — a sheet of nothing but passes reads as a pass for the whole unit, which is the error the printed report exists to avoid. JSON is the same data with the flags and timestamps intact, for anything that reads the file rather than looks at it. Both are generated here and saved by your browser; nothing is uploaded.

The report never invents a result. A test you did not run is listed as not tested rather than assumed good, because “not tested” and “passed” are very different things to put in front of a buyer. Nothing leaves this machine — printing goes to your own printer or PDF writer, and copying goes to your clipboard.

Caps, Num and Scroll Lock cannot be held inside the page — the keyboard flips them before any website sees the key. So they are graded on what matters: the lock has to change state, not just send a keypress. One that reports a press but never moves the light is dead. Anything left on is called out in the verdict.

Capture mode needs Chrome, Edge or Opera for the full key hold. In Firefox and Safari the page still reads every key, but the operating system may take Windows/Command and some F-keys.

A refurbished board that types clean at speed is a board that passes. Watch for letters that drop out entirely, or one that repeats — those show up as mistakes here long before you notice them by eye.

Rollover & ghosting

Hold down as many keys at once as you can — all four fingers, then both hands. A cheap membrane board stops registering at 2–3 keys. A proper mechanical one takes six or more.

If it stops at exactly six, that is almost certainly not the keyboard. USB keyboards have two report modes. In boot protocol — the simple one a BIOS can read — the report has room for six keys plus modifiers, full stop. Many boards only switch to the richer mode when a driver asks, and some operating systems never ask. So six is a number the protocol imposes, not one the switches do. Modifiers travel in their own field and do not count against it. A board stopping at two or three is a real limit worth recording; one stopping at six is a note for your listing, not a fault.

Earbuds & authenticity

Measures the drivers against a pair you know is genuine, checks the sensors behave like real ones, and watches for a bud dropping out.

No browser can read a serial number, firmware version or anything else from Apple. Nothing here talks to Apple and nothing here is proof on its own. What it gives you is a confidence score from things that can be measured — drivers, sensors, and behaviour — which you weigh alongside the case, the engraving and the price you paid.
  1. 1Connect the earbuds and set them as the computer's output
  2. 2Rest one bud directly on the laptop's microphone hole
  3. 3Run the sweep and read the score

Listen with must be the laptop's own microphone, not the earbuds. The moment earbuds become the input device they drop into headset mode — mono, and everything above about 8 kHz thrown away — which ruins both the playback and the measurement.

Capture a reference

Do this once per model, with a pair whose provenance you are sure about — sealed, or bought from Apple. Everything you test afterwards is scored against it.

Capture it the same way you will test: same bud position, same microphone, same room. The comparison is only as good as how repeatable your placement is.

Saved references

Profiles live in this browser on this machine. Export once and import on every other bench PC so all of them judge against the same pair.

Ear detection

Genuine AirPods pause playback when a bud comes out. All this page can see is that something paused playback — a Bluetooth dropout or an output-device change looks identical to the browser, and no browser can read the wear sensor itself. Put both in, press start, then take one out, and repeat it two or three times: pausing every time you remove a bud and never when you leave it alone is the pattern worth trusting. One pause on its own is not.

One honest catch: if automatic ear detection is switched off in the phone or computer settings, a genuine pair fails this too. Check the setting before you judge it.

A bud that dies after fifteen minutes is the most common fault on used earbuds and the easiest one to miss. Start this, play music through them, and leave it.

Serial check

Apple’s older serial numbers are not random — they encode the factory, the half-year and the week the unit was built. This reads those out, checks the whole thing is a shape Apple actually uses, and cross-checks the date against the model you picked. It runs entirely on this machine and contacts nobody.

Shape
—
Built
—
Factory
—
Against the model
—
Read this once and you will never misuse the result. A serial that passes this check is not proven genuine — a counterfeiter can print a correctly-shaped serial as easily as a wrong one, and plenty do. What this catches is the other half: invented serials, mistyped ones, an O typed for a zero, and the contradiction where the encoded build date predates the model it is printed on. A fail here is worth acting on. A pass only means move on to the next check. For the authoritative answer, use the button above and read it from Apple yourself — no browser can ask them on your behalf.

Serial log

Read the serial off the case lid and type it in. This is a memory aid, not a verdict: the usual reason a serial comes back twice is that you are re-testing the same unit, and the log counts the repeat rather than flagging it. It only points at a fake when two different physical pairs carry the same serial — that is the signal to act on.

Result

Logged so far
0

Kept on this machine only, capped at the last 500 entries, and cleared by the button above or by “Delete everything” on the System page. This checks your own history only — it never contacts Apple, and it cannot tell you whether a serial is valid, only whether you have seen it before. To verify one properly, type it into Apple's own coverage checker yourself.

What the computer cannot check

  • engravingInside the case lid, under a loupe. Genuine text is crisp and evenly spaced. Fakes are dotty, shallow or slightly crooked.
  • hingeMetal, firm, and it stops cleanly. A loose or plasticky hinge with a soft stop is the single fastest tell.
  • weightWeigh your sealed reference pair and its case, write the numbers on the bench. Counterfeits are almost always lighter — compare against your own known-good figures, not against numbers off the internet.
  • meshThe speaker and microphone grilles are a fine, even mesh set flush. Fakes use coarser mesh, often sitting slightly proud or recessed.
  • magnetsBuds snap into the case decisively and the lid pulls itself shut. Weak or vague magnets mean cheap ones.
  • pairingOn an iPhone, a genuine pair raises the full pairing card with the correct model name and an animation. Fakes often show a generic card, the wrong name, or nothing at all.
  • squeezeOn Pro models the stem squeeze gives a distinct click through the bud. Touch-only controls with no click are a strong tell.

How to weigh it all up

No single check here is conclusive, including the sweep. Faults cluster, and so do fakes.

  • send backDriver response more than 6 dB out, and ear detection does nothing, and the hinge feels wrong. Three independent signals agreeing is as close to certain as you will get without Apple.
  • look againOne signal fails and the rest pass. Re-seat the bud and sweep again, check the ear-detection setting is actually on, and look at the engraving before you decide.
  • sell itResponse within 3 dB, ear detection pauses, serial not seen before, case and engraving clean, and both buds survive a dropout watch.

Keep the sealed reference pair in a drawer and do not sell it. It is a measuring instrument now, and it is worth more to you than its resale value.

Screens

Monitors

Full-screen patterns for dead pixels, backlight bleed, banding and ghosting. Run the whole set automatically, or pick one.

Dead pixel check

The fastest check there is, and the one you run first. The whole screen fills with one colour; click or press any key and it moves to the next. Red, green, blue, white, black. A dead pixel stays black on every one of them. A stuck pixel stays its own colour on every one of them. Dust wipes off and a fault does not — so if something survives all five and a wipe, it is the panel.

not running

It goes full screen, so drag this window onto the monitor you are testing first. Esc or a right-click leaves at any point, and the colour you were on is remembered for the report.

Refresh rate is measured live over one second. Drag this window onto the monitor you are testing before you read it.

Before you run these on a shop floor: the stuck-pixel flush flashes the whole screen through saturated colours at two changes a second. That is under the three-per-second limit published in WCAG 2.3.1, but “under the limit” is not the same as safe for everyone — if anyone nearby is photosensitive or has epilepsy, do not run it while they are in the room. It arms on the first press and runs on the second so you cannot start it by mis-clicking. Every other pattern on this page is still or slow-moving.

Automatic run

The full run walks all eleven colour fields and all ten patterns on its own — twenty-one steps. About two minutes at six seconds each, or twenty seconds flat at one. One second is a fast sweep for catching a dead pixel or a backlight fault; six is the right dwell for banding, uniformity and near-black crush, which your eyes need a moment to settle into. Space pauses, → skips, ← goes back, Esc stops.

Solid fields

A dead pixel stays black on every field. A stuck pixel stays one colour on every field. Dust wipes off; a fault does not.

Single patterns

Stuck-pixel flush cycles the whole screen through saturated colours twice a second; leave it running ten minutes on a stuck subpixel. It flashes — press the button once to arm it, again to run, and skip it entirely if anyone nearby is photosensitive.

Privacy & data

The short version: nothing you do on this page leaves this computer. There is no account, no analytics, no tracking, no cookies and no third-party code of any kind — the site makes zero requests to anyone but itself. Below is every single thing it keeps, where it keeps it, and a button that removes all of it.

Counting…

What never happens here

  • networkNo request goes anywhere except back to this site for its own files. No fonts, no scripts, no beacons, no CDN. The one exception is the router page, which deliberately fetches a file from this same site to time it — you press the button and it tells you how much it pulled.
  • microphoneAudio is analysed live in the browser and thrown away frame by frame. Nothing is written to disk and nothing is sent anywhere. The recorder on the audio page makes a clip you can play back in the tab; it is gone when you close it unless you save it yourself.
  • cameraThe preview is drawn straight from the camera. Pressing Snapshot paints one frame into a canvas on the page; it is not saved or uploaded. Leaving the camera page switches the camera off.
  • serialsSerial numbers you type on the earbuds page are stored on this machine so repeats stand out, and nowhere else. They are capped at 500 entries, oldest dropped first, and the delete button above clears them.
  • cookiesNone are set, so there is nothing to consent to. The theme choice and the serial log use local storage, which is per-machine and never transmitted with a request.
  • permissionsMicrophone, camera, gamepad, HID and MIDI are only requested when you press the button that needs them, and the browser asks you first every time it has to. Revoke any of them from the padlock in the address bar; nothing here can grant itself access.

Who runs this

Operated by
The bench operator who deployed it. This is private tooling, not a public service, and it is deliberately not linked to any trading name — a tool that tells every visitor whose shop it belongs to is a lead nobody asked to publish.
What it is for
Testing used and returned hardware before it is listed, refurbished or scrapped. An internal bench tool — not a product, not a service offered to anyone, and nothing on it is for sale.
Who it is for
Bench staff on the shop floor. Nobody signs up, nothing is sold through it, no payment is taken and no money changes hands anywhere on this site — which is why there is no refund policy, no terms of sale and no cookie banner to accept. Those exist to govern a transaction, and there is no transaction here.
Not suitable for children
It is a workshop tool for adults handling returned stock. No part of it is aimed at or marketed to children, and it collects nothing about anyone.
Data requests
There is no server and no database, so there is nothing held about you anywhere for anyone to look up, export or delete on request. Everything there is sits on the machine in front of you and the button above removes it.
Search engines
Told to stay away, in all three places that matter: robots.txt, an X-Robots-Tag header on every response, and a noindex meta in the page for when it is served without headers. Honestly though: those are requests, and a crawler that ignores them meets no obstacle. The reason that is acceptable is that there is nothing here worth taking — no server, no database, no customer records, no credentials, and every internal note kept out of the deployment.
Fonts and images
Every typeface is one your operating system already ships. Every icon on the site is hand-drawn SVG in the page itself. Nothing is licensed from anyone and nothing is hot-linked.

Green line is response time, second by second. Every red column is a moment the router did not answer at all. One red column on a five-minute soak is a router you send back.

Speed test

Three numbers, in one run. Download speed, how long the line takes to answer when it is idle, and — the one most speed tests leave out — how long it takes to answer while it is busy. That third number is the one that explains a call that breaks up whenever somebody starts a download, and it is the fastest way to tell a bad router from a slow line.

Honest about what this is: a download measurement against this site, so it is capped by the shop's internet and by this machine's Wi-Fi, and it cannot prove a router is capable of gigabit. It is very good at the opposite — showing one crawling at 3 Mbps on a line that does fifty, or one whose response time climbs from 12 ms to 400 ms the moment traffic starts. Upload is not measured, and no static site can measure it: there is no server here to accept the data. Every byte this pulls is counted and shown above, and it all stops the moment you leave the page.

Stress test

Loads every CPU core and the graphics chip, then watches the frame rate. A machine that throttles, crashes or drops off a cliff under load has a cooling or power fault you will not find by opening the lid.

This deliberately heats the machine and spins the fans up. Run it on a bench, not on a lap, and stop it if anything smells hot or the machine shuts down.

GPU load

Idle The shader draws here while the test runs.

The picture is meaningless on purpose — an interference pattern recomputed for every pixel, every frame, to keep the graphics chip busy. What matters is that it keeps moving. Stutter, tearing or a freeze while the clock keeps climbing means the chip is unstable under load. Raise Graphics load if a machine sails through.

How to read it

  • goodFrame rate holds flat for the whole run and the fans settle. Cooling is doing its job.
  • throttleFrame rate starts high then steps down after thirty to ninety seconds. That is thermal throttling — dust, dried paste, or a fan not spinning.
  • faultLong stalls, the image freezing, the tab crashing or the machine restarting. Power delivery, memory or the graphics chip.

Browsers cannot read temperatures or fan speeds, so this measures the symptom rather than the cause. For actual sensor numbers you still need a tool on the machine itself.
